definition.text: A sunk cost is money, time or effort already spent that cannot be recovered.

facts.text: It contrasts with prospective costs, future costs that can still be avoided by acting.
Standard economic theory holds that only future costs matter to a rational decision; this is called the bygones principle or marginal principle.

A factory expected to cost $100 million and yield $120 million should be abandoned if, after $30 million is spent, its value projection falls to $65 million, since finishing would cost $70 million more.
If the projection instead falls to $75 million, a rational company should continue the project.
In everyday life people often let past spending, for example on repairing a car or house, shape their future decisions.

definition.text: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to keep going with something because of what has already been invested in it, even when stopping would be better.

facts.text: It is described as 'throwing good money after bad' instead of 'cutting one's losses'.
Managers of many US utility companies were found to be overly reluctant to end economically unviable nuclear plant projects.
Behavioural economics links it to framing effects, overoptimism, a sense of personal responsibility and the wish not to appear wasteful.
In one study, managers told they had made an earlier poor investment put in an average of $12.97 million more, versus $9.43 million for those told someone else had.

definition.text: The utility maximization problem describes how a consumer chooses the most preferred bundle of goods they can afford with limited income at given prices.

facts.text: It assumes the consumer can rank every possible bundle by the utility it gives.
It gives a systematic account of consumer demand and how it changes when income or prices change.
The constraint reflects scarcity; besides money, consumers may face time constraints and budgets spread over time.
If all prices and income rise at the same rate, the affordable set and the best choice stay the same.
Because of bounded rationality, such as lack of time or information, real consumers sometimes pick bundles that do not maximize utility.
The problem was first developed by the utilitarian philosophers Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill.

definition.text: Absolute advantage is the ability of a person, firm or country to produce a good or service more efficiently than others.

facts.text: Adam Smith first described it in The Wealth of Nations in 1776, arguing against mercantilism that all nations could gain from free trade and specialization.
If the UK needs fewer hours to make cloth and Portugal fewer to make wine, specializing and trading leaves both with more of each good.
A party can have no absolute advantage in anything yet still gain from trade through comparative advantage.
